lesson.arabic-greetings-address.title_en: Talking to a man or a woman: أَنْتَ and أَنْتِ
lesson.arabic-greetings-address.family_en: "You" and "your" change for a man or a woman
steps: When you talk to one person, Arabic has two words for "you": أَنْتَ to a man and أَنْتِ to a woman. Only the last vowel differs: -ta or -ti.
"Your" works the same way, as an ending on the word: -ka to a man, -ki to a woman. اِسْمُكَ is "your name" to a man, and اِسْمُكِ to a woman.
So the question changes with the person you ask: كَيْفَ حَالُكَ؟ to a man, كَيْفَ حَالُكِ؟ to a woman.
Without vowel marks the two look alike, so the last vowel is what you listen for.
أَنَا, "I", is the same word for a man or a woman, and so is بِخَيْرٍ: أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ, I'm well, doesn't change. Some other words about yourself do: طَالِب for a man, طَالِبَة for a woman.

examples.en: My name's Laylā, and what's yours? (to a man)
You're a student, and you're a teacher.

why.q_en: Why does Arabic need two words for "you"?
why.a_en: Arabic shows whether you're talking to a man or a woman, in "you", in "your" and in many verbs. It isn't about politeness: both forms are equally polite.

selftest.q_en: You're asking a woman how she is. What do you say?
selftest.why_en: To a woman, "your" is -ki: حَالُكِ. -ka is for a man, and حَالِي is "my state".

selftest.q_en: Which word means "you" when you speak to a man?
selftest.why_en: أَنْتَ, with -ta, is for a man; أَنْتِ, with -ti, for a woman. أَنَا is "I".

selftest.q_en: Does أَنَا بِخَيْرٍ change when a woman says it?
choices: No, it's the same for a man or a woman
selftest.answer: No, it's the same for a man or a woman
selftest.why_en: Neither أَنَا nor بِخَيْرٍ changes for a man or a woman, so the whole phrase stays the same.

leads_to.en: Verbs split for a man or a woman too: تَكْتُبُ, تَكْتُبِينَ.

lesson.arabic-greetings-address.family_en: Each greeting has its own answer
steps: Arabic greetings come in pairs: each one has its own reply, so learn them together.
Many replies answer with something brighter: صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ, "morning of good", is answered with صَبَاحُ النُّورِ, "morning of light".
السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ works anywhere, with anyone. The reply turns the words round and adds وَ, "and": وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ.
عَلَيْكُمْ is plural, but it's used for one person too.
When someone thanks you with شُكْرًا, the answer is عَفْوًا, you're welcome.

examples.en: Welcome to our home. (to a woman)

why.q_en: Why isn't صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ answered with the same words?
why.a_en: It's the custom: the reply matches the greeting and goes one better, "light" for "good". Saying صَبَاحُ الْخَيْرِ back wouldn't be wrong, but صَبَاحُ النُّورِ is what people expect.

selftest.q_en: Someone says مَسَاءُ الْخَيْرِ. What's the usual reply?
selftest.why_en: مَسَاءُ is evening, so the reply is مَسَاءُ النُّورِ. صَبَاحُ النُّورِ is for the morning, and مَعَ السَّلَامَةِ means goodbye.

selftest.q_en: What's the reply to السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكُمْ?
selftest.why_en: The reply turns the words round and adds وَ: وَعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلَامُ.

selftest.q_en: Someone says شُكْرًا to you. What do you answer?
selftest.why_en: عَفْوًا is "you're welcome". It's also "excuse me" or "sorry".

leads_to.en: After hello: short words that keep a conversation going.

lesson.arabic-nominal-sentences.title_en: Saying what something is, with no "is"
lesson.arabic-nominal-sentences.family_en: A sentence without a verb: what you're talking about, and what you say about it

table.form_en: a phrase, not yet a sentence

steps: In the present, Arabic doesn't need a word for "is" or "are": أَنَا طَالِبٌ is "I (am) a student".
A sentence like this has two parts: what you're talking about, and what you say about it.
With الْـ on the first word and none on the second, it's a sentence: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ, the house is big.
With الْـ on both, it's a phrase, not yet a sentence: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ, the big house. Add something to make it one: الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ جَدِيدٌ.
For a woman, or a feminine word, the second part usually ends in ة: هِيَ طَبِيبَةٌ; الْغُرْفَةُ صَغِيرَةٌ.

examples.en: I'm an engineer and she's a doctor.

words.en: (is) small (with ة: the room is feminine)
the new one (with الْـ: part of the phrase)
(is) beautiful (no الْـ: what you say about it)

why.q_en: With no "is", how can I tell a sentence from a phrase?
why.a_en: Look at the second word. If it has الْـ like the first (الْبَيْتُ الْكَبِيرُ), it belongs to the name: the big house. If it has no الْـ (الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ), it's what you're saying about the house: the house is big.

selftest.q_en: What does الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ mean?
selftest.why_en: Only the first word has الْـ, so it's a sentence: the book (is) new.

selftest.q_en: Which is a full sentence?
selftest.why_en: الْقَلَمُ صَغِيرٌ is "the pen is small". The other two are phrases: "the small pen" and "a small pen".

selftest.q_en: A man says "I'm busy". Which is it?
selftest.why_en: مَشْغُولَةٌ is what a woman says, and أَنْتَ مَشْغُولٌ is "you're busy".

leads_to.en: كَانَ puts these sentences into the past.

lesson.arabic-simple-questions.title_en: Question words: هَلْ, مَنْ, مَا, أَيْنَ, مَتَى, كَيْفَ
lesson.arabic-simple-questions.family_en: Asking for the piece of information you need
steps: Choose the question word for what you're missing: a person (مَنْ), a thing (مَا), a place (أَيْنَ), a time (مَتَى) or a way (كَيْفَ).
هَلْ at the start turns a statement into a yes/no question: هَلْ أَنْتَ طَالِبٌ؟ The answer is نَعَمْ, yes, or لَا, no.
مَا is "what" before a noun or a pronoun (مَا هَذَا؟), and مَاذَا before a verb (مَاذَا تَدْرُسُ؟).
Before الْـ, هَلْ takes a helping i: هَلِ الْكِتَابُ جَدِيدٌ؟
The question word comes first, and the rest stays as it would in a statement: الْبَيْتُ هُنَا, the house is here; أَيْنَ الْبَيْتُ؟, where is the house?

words.en: (starts a yes/no question; the i joins it to the next word)

why.q_en: Why don't Arabic questions need "is" or "does"?
why.a_en: Just as in statements: أَيْنَ الْبَيْتُ؟ is literally "where the house?", and هَلْ تَدْرُسُ؟ is "do you study?" with no word for "do". The question word does the job.

selftest.q_en: You want to know when the train leaves. Which word do you start with?
selftest.why_en: مَتَى asks about a time. أَيْنَ asks where, and مَنْ who.

selftest.q_en: Which word for "what" goes before a verb?
selftest.why_en: مَاذَا goes before a verb (مَاذَا تَدْرُسُ؟), and مَا before a noun or a pronoun (مَا هَذَا؟).

selftest.q_en: Which is a natural answer to هَلْ أَنْتِ مَشْغُولَةٌ؟
selftest.why_en: A هَلْ question is answered with نَعَمْ or لَا, and you answer about yourself with أَنَا.

leads_to.en: The same question words with past verbs.

lesson.arabic-origin-location.title_en: In, from, to, on: فِي, مِنْ, إِلَى, عَلَى
lesson.arabic-origin-location.family_en: Small words for place, and the -i ending after them

table.en: away from the house; about the house

steps: These small words show where something is, where it comes from or where it's going: فِي, in; مِنْ, from; إِلَى, to; عَلَى, on.
The noun after them ends in -i: فِي الْبَيْتِ, عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ. Without الْـ, it ends in -in: فِي بَيْتٍ, in a house.
Before الْـ, مِنْ becomes مِنَ and عَنْ becomes عَنِ, so the words run on smoothly: مِنَ الْمَدْرَسَةِ, عَنِ الْبَيْتِ.
Where you are and where you're from are different questions: أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ asks where you are now; مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتَ؟ asks where you're from.
إِلَى is for moving towards a place: أَذْهَبُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ, I go to school. For being in a place, use فِي.

examples.ar: أَنَا مِنْ لُبْنَانَ، وَأَسْكُنُ فِي بِرِيطَانِيَا.
examples.en: I'm from Lebanon, and I live in Britain.

words.en: Lebanon (a name like this takes -a here, not -i, and never -in)

examples.en: The pen is on the table.
The school is near the house.

words.en: from (English just says "near the house"; مِنْ becomes مِنَ before الْـ)

why.q_en: Why does the noun end in -i after فِي?
why.a_en: These little words always put the noun after them in its -i form; it's one of the main jobs of the endings. So the same word can end differently: الْبَيْتُ كَبِيرٌ, the house is big, but فِي الْبَيْتِ, in the house.

selftest.q_en: Which ending does a noun take after عَلَى?
selftest.why_en: After فِي, مِنْ, عَلَى and the other small place words, the noun ends in -i: عَلَى الْمَكْتَبِ.

selftest.q_en: "I'm going to the market": which word means "to"?
selftest.why_en: إِلَى is for moving towards a place. فِي is "in", and مِنْ is "from".

selftest.q_en: What does مِنْ أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟ ask?
selftest.why_en: مِنْ أَيْنَ is "from where". "Where are you?" is أَيْنَ أَنْتِ؟

leads_to.en: Which small word a verb takes after it.

lesson.arabic-origin-location.title_en: From a place to a describing word: مِصْر, مِصْرِيّ
lesson.arabic-origin-location.family_en: Adding ـِيّ to a place makes "from there"

table.form_en: a man from there (the ـا drops)

steps: To say someone is from a place, add ـِيّ to the place's name: مِصْر, Egypt; مِصْرِيّ, Egyptian.
For a woman, add ـِيَّة instead: مِصْرِيَّة.
If the country's name has الْـ, leave it off: الْعِرَاق, عِرَاقِيّ. If it ends in ـا, drop that too: بِرِيطَانِيَا, بِرِيطَانِيّ.
Use it like any describing word: هُوَ مِصْرِيٌّ وَهِيَ لُبْنَانِيَّةٌ, he's Egyptian and she's Lebanese.
The same ending makes describing words from other nouns too: عَرَبِيّ, Arab or Arabic, from عَرَب, the Arabs.

examples.en: I'm British, and my friend is Iraqi.
She's from Syria, so she's Syrian.

why.q_en: Why is it عِرَاقِيّ, without الْـ, when the country is الْعِرَاق?
why.a_en: The describing word is made from the name itself, without "the". You add الْـ again only when the phrase needs it, as in الطَّالِبُ الْعِرَاقِيُّ, the Iraqi student.

selftest.q_en: How does a woman from Lebanon describe herself?
selftest.why_en: For a woman, the ending is ـِيَّة. The other two are the word for a man and the name of the country.

selftest.q_en: Which means "Iraqi" for a man?
selftest.why_en: الْعِرَاق is the country, and عِرَاقِيَّة is for a woman.

selftest.q_en: What do you add to a place's name to make "from there", for a man?
selftest.why_en: ـِيّ makes "from there" (ـِيَّة for a woman). ـَة marks the feminine, and ـَات a plural.

leads_to.en: Describing words come after their noun and match it.

lesson.arabic-repair-phrases.title_en: When you don't understand: asking politely
lesson.arabic-repair-phrases.family_en: Phrases that keep a conversation going, to a man or a woman
steps: Not understanding is a normal part of talking in a new language. Say so, and ask for what you need.
Start with عَفْوًا, excuse me, or لَمْ أَفْهَمْ, I didn't understand.
Then ask: أَعِدْ, repeat, and add بِبُطْءٍ, slowly, or مَرَّةً أُخْرَى, once more. Finish with مِنْ فَضْلِكَ, please.
To a woman, the request ends in -ī: أَعِيدِي, and "please" is مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.
For one word you didn't catch, ask about it: مَا مَعْنَى هَذِهِ الْكَلِمَةِ؟

examples.ar: عَفْوًا، أَعِيدِي مَرَّةً أُخْرَى، مِنْ فَضْلِكِ.
examples.en: Excuse me, could you say it again, please? (to a woman)

words.en: word (the -a ending: what I didn't understand)

why.q_en: Isn't it rude to keep asking someone to repeat?
why.a_en: No: asking shows you're listening and want to understand, and it keeps the conversation honest. A polite عَفْوًا at the start and مِنْ فَضْلِكَ at the end is all it takes.

selftest.q_en: How do you ask a woman to repeat?
selftest.why_en: To a woman the request ends in -ī: أَعِيدِي. أَعِدْ is to a man, and أُعِيدُ means "I repeat".

selftest.q_en: What does بِبُطْءٍ add to a request?
selftest.why_en: بِبُطْءٍ is "slowly". "Again" is مَرَّةً أُخْرَى, and "please" is مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.

selftest.q_en: Which question asks what a word means?
selftest.why_en: مَعْنَى is "meaning". The others ask your name and when the lesson is.

leads_to.en: Why it's لَمْ أَفْهَمْ, with a present verb, for "I didn't understand".
